analysis.one_liner: Requires agencies to prove major rules' benefits outweigh their costs before issuing them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote; it had just one cosponsor and no floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal agencies to determine that a rule's benefits justify its costs before proposing or finalizing any major rule, and to complete a detailed regulatory impact analysis for rules with $100 million or more in annual economic effects [S2][S3]. It would have let courts review those analyses, required agencies to prefer the "least burdensome" option, and required agencies to consider expiration dates for major rules [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses — energy, manufacturing, chemical, pharmaceutical, and financial firms — would gain. Every major rule would have to pass a benefit-cost test, and agencies would have to choose the least burdensome option and weigh the cumulative burden of all rules on the regulated company [S2][S3]. Opening the analyses to judicial review would give companies a new way to sue to delay or overturn rules they dislike [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Agencies could issue a major rule only after a reasoned determination that its benefits justify its costs, giving regulated companies a legal hook to challenge rules that impose costs on them [S2][S3].

For economically significant rules — generally those with $100 million or more in annual effects — agencies would have to complete a detailed regulatory impact analysis covering costs, alternatives including not regulating, effects on different sizes of businesses, and the cumulative burden of other rules on the same companies; courts could review that analysis [S2][S3].

If an agency picked an approach more burdensome than an available alternative, it would have to say so and justify it, and agencies would have to consider sunset dates that could let major rules expire [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public, through potentially weaker or slower health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections. Many benefits of protective rules — lives saved, illnesses prevented, cleaner air and water — are hard to put a dollar figure on, so a mandatory benefit-cost gate and court review tend to fall hardest on protective rules while costs to companies are easier to count [S3]. Taxpayers would also bear the cost of added litigation over agency analyses [S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring agencies to show benefits justify costs before issuing any major rule biases the process against protective regulation, because the benefits of rules — prevented deaths, illnesses, and pollution — are difficult to quantify and monetize while industry compliance costs are easy to count [S3].

Opening regulatory impact analyses to judicial review would let regulated companies sue over the paperwork behind rules, adding years of delay to protections that already take years to finalize [S2][S3].
A statutory preference for the least burdensome alternative and mandatory sunset consideration could force agencies to weaken rules or let them lapse even where stronger protection is warranted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Requiring agencies to publish transparent, replicable cost-benefit analyses has some genuine transparency value for the public [S2]. But the bill's enforceable core — a benefit-justifies-cost gate, a least-burdensome preference, and court review of the analyses — mainly hands regulated industries litigation tools and procedural roadblocks, while the benefits of protective rules are systematically the hardest side of the ledger to prove [S3]. On balance the bill was designed to slow and lighten regulation far more than to inform the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on March 16, 2023, with Sen. James Lankford as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day; no markup, hearing vote, or floor action ever followed [S5].
With no committee action and no vote in either chamber, the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and the existing body of public protections came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, no new benefit-cost gate, least-burdensome mandate, or litigation avenue was created for regulated companies to use against rules on health, safety, and the environment.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: Senate Republican Conference Chair; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its cost-benefit and judicial-review requirements for federal rulemaking

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (Chair Gary Peters)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no markup or committee vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no position can be measured; both sponsors were Republicans, and the bill never advanced out of a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would have required every major rule to pass a benefit-cost test, weighed the cumulative burden of all rules on regulated companies, preferred the least burdensome option, and let courts review the analyses — a toolkit for delaying, weakening, or striking rules these companies dislike. Its death leaves the current rulemaking process unchanged.

The bill would have added statutory constraints — mandatory impact analyses, a benefits-justify-costs determination, and sunset consideration — to how agencies write major rules. Because it died, agencies' existing authority and process are untouched.
